name: Astrid Sonne
label: Escho
lede: Astrid Sonne left the classical track at 18, taught herself Ableton by trial and error, and years of instrumentals later sang her own songs on Great Doubt, which Pitchfork ranked No. 9 on its year-end 50.

eras.title: Christmas trees and a viola
eras.text: Sonne grows up on the Danish island of Bornholm, where her family runs a Christmas tree business, and starts viola at six. At 16 she moves to Copenhagen for classical training; at 18 she walks away from it.

years.h: Born on Bornholm, handed a viola at six
years.p: Astrid Sonne grows up on the Danish island of Bornholm, sings in a church as a teenager and plays viola from age six.
years.xp: Dazed reports that her family runs a Christmas tree business on the island, and that she worked as a church singer through her teens before heading to Copenhagen. Fact adds that she trained rigorously on viola from the start.

years.big: "I didn't want any help. Essentially, I'm just a really stubborn person."
years.h: Sonne quits classical training and opens Ableton
years.p: She told Fact she skipped the tutorials after leaving a strict pre-conservatory programme at 18. Trial and error did the rest.
years.xp:
She had moved to Copenhagen at 16. Explaining the break, she told Fact: "I couldn't really express the things I wanted to express." Once she found out she could make music herself, she began experimenting, first locking herself in a rehearsal room with the viola, then buying pedals, then finding her way to the computer.

An early spark was the politically charged electronic music of the Danish producer HVAD. Laurel Halo and Steve Reich came later as reference points. She went on to graduate from Copenhagen's Rhythmic Music Conservatory, per Dazed.

eras.title: Escho, then the critics
eras.text: Escho, a Copenhagen label home to the city's experimental scene, releases her debut, and live viola goes up against synthesizers. Danish critics notice fast.

years.cap: Astrid Sonne at a Posh Isolation night at Mayhem, Copenhagen
years.h: Human Lines sets a choir sample against a dubstep synth
years.p: Her debut on Escho is built on live viola and pedals. Fact rated her a daring new experimenter.
years.xp:
Sonne told Fact the idea was simple: "I really wanted to experiment with what happens when you take a choir sample and put it together with a dubstep synth."

The album runs from minimal bleeps to lush string arrangements.

years.h: Crack covers "Strong, Calm, Slow" ahead of the Cliodynamics EP
years.p: The EP follows two singles, "Area Under a Curve" and "Strong, Calm, Slow."

years.cap: Astrid Sonne at Alice's Summer Series, Copenhagen, July 2020
years.h: Danish critics name her Composer of the Year
years.p: The Steppeulven Danish Music Critic Prize goes to Sonne in 2020, and again in 2022, per her own site.
years.xp: Her site also lists a special mention at the Nordic Music Prize in 2022. In 2020 she appeared on the compilation Kulør 006, per Wikipedia.

eras.title: A bigger circle
eras.text: The second album brings in guitar, organ, voices and friends from the Copenhagen scene, and puts her on the international radar.

years.cap: Astrid Sonne at Gong Tomorrow Music festival, Copenhagen, September 2021
years.h: [[ML Buch|e0f9a19e-a929-4a9f-a5dc-82b2d305f03d]] plays guitar on outside of your lifetime, and an organ joins
years.p: Ten short tracks of synthesizers, strings, drones and choral harmony. Minais B plays the organ and Tobias Kropp sings, per Boomkat.
years.xp:
Pitchfork put the album in its "Great Records You May Have Missed" for autumn 2021, and both Pitchfork and Paste named it among the year's best electronic records, per Wikipedia.

Boomkat's description points to sequencers tied to esoteric algorithms, fugues in flux and free jazz. It is her last record before she starts writing songs.

years.h: Pitchfork puts Ephemeral Camera Feed on its mid-year list
years.p: It reviews the EP in April, then slots it into its best albums of 2022 so far in June.

eras.title: Her own voice
eras.text: After years of instrumentals, Sonne sings her own songs, from a new base in London. A Copenhagen experimentalist turns into a year-end-list regular.

years.cap: Astrid Sonne at LEV Festival, April 2023
years.h: The Lot Radio in Brooklyn gets her live set, ten months before Great Doubt
years.p: The March 26 broadcast catches the set as her music turns toward song.

years.cap: Astrid Sonne's Great Doubt show, Copenhagen Distillery, February 2024
years.src: Album of the Year · Dazed · The Vinyl Factory
years.h: Pitchfork gives Great Doubt 7.7 and a No. 9 on its year-end 50
years.p: Her first album of proper songs puts her voice over viola, woodwinds and harp loops.
years.xp:
Philip Sherburne's Pitchfork review scored the album 77 out of 100, per Album of the Year, which also lists The Guardian at 80, No. 3 at The Vinyl Factory and No. 4 at Resident Advisor. Pitchfork's summary said she turns toward singer-songwriter introspection, finding drama and yearning in understated arrangements.

Dazed described staccato sequencers and jagged structures under gentle vocals. She told The Vinyl Factory that music made "out of duty" wasn't her best work, and that a more relaxed approach followed that realisation.

years.big: "A quite energetic track coming from a not very energetic place."
years.h: Sonne makes "Boost" without getting out of bed
years.p: Stereogum runs the single on January 10, sixteen days before the album.
years.xp: Sonne told Stereogum: "I made 'Boost' lying in my bed." She described the track as having a sense of release and of not caring too much, which she said can help when you need to seek out new settings.

years.cap: ML Buch at Elsewhere, Brooklyn, June 2024
years.h: Sonne and Buch tour the UK with one new record each
years.p: The March run includes Glasgow's Flying Duck, with Sonne playing Great Doubt and [[ML Buch|e0f9a19e-a929-4a9f-a5dc-82b2d305f03d]] playing Suntub.
years.xp:
Talkhouse caught them on the phone before the tour. Buch had urged Sonne years earlier to try songwriting, which she first resisted. Sonne called releasing her first proper songs "really daunting," then found the other side of it on stage: "People were singing the lyrics - I have never experienced that before."

Both had left Copenhagen for room to work: Sonne to London, Buch to three years in the countryside.

eras.title: Friends rebuild it, then a church
eras.text: Friends take the album apart, a duo appears, and Sonne carries a stripped-down string trio across North America.

years.h: Sonne and Fine Glindvad start Coined
years.p: Their song "Your House" gets pickups from The Face and Paper the same month.

years.h: Blood Orange, Smerz and HVAD rework Great Doubt as "edits"
years.p: Sonne also asks ML Buch, Valentina Magaletti and Lolina, and steers away from the word remix.
years.xp:
She told Clash the word was chosen so the artists would feel as free as possible with the material. The set includes an off-kilter duet with Blood Orange, a sustained dubplate loop by HVAD and an orchestral introduction by ML Buch.

A video for "Staying here," assembled from fan footage of her summer shows, came out the same day.

yt: "Do You Wanna" at Pioneer Works, March 25
years.h: Knoxville's First Presbyterian Sanctuary hosts her string trio
years.p: At Big Ears, Sonne plays with violinist Magdalena McLean and cellist Emma Barnaby, working a mixer with close to 100 mappings.
years.xp:
She told The Fader why she brought strings: "I was trying to get away from the table. When you do electronic music, there's this wall between you and the audience." The set ran an hour, with the audience seated. She had played Brooklyn days earlier and said going "full-on crazy" in the church wouldn't have fitted the vibe.

On being seen as a pop figure after Great Doubt, she said: "It's very weird having people perceive me in that way." Next on her list were more Coined work with Glindvad and work with producer Loraine James.
